subsubtopic: PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF SECURITY, CONTROL AND CONDITIONS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA INSTITUTION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the tragic event that has just taken place in the British Columbia penitentiary in which three prisoners known to be dangerous and serving life imprisonment entered an area of classification together while carrying concealed weapons and held a number of employees of the institution as hostages, one of the hostages losing her life, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That the government immediately set up a royal commission with terms of reference to investigate the whole tragic affair, the security, control and conditions of the said British Columbia penitentiary, to determine, first, the cause of this uncontrolled violence, and to report on decisions made that brought this sad tragedy to an end, with the authority to look into the security and control of all penitentiaries in Canada and the general conditions existing therein.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In the past it has been the practice for the Ministry of Finance to act as the official government organ responsible for evaluation, forecasting and policy concerning the Canadian economy. Considering that a quasi-autonomous Crown corporation, CMHC, whose membership includes the deputy minister of finance, has issued a report the contents of which tend to contradict reports put forward previously by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in that it predicts a higher rate of unemployment, higher mortgage rates and fewer housing starts than the projections previously provided to this House, I move seconded by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens):

REASON FOR DELAY IN BUILDING NEW PENAL INSTITUTIONS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
In
view of the fact that the real problem in British Columbia is the lack of new penitentiary facilities and the fact the government has not been able to get under construction the two maximum security institutions they indicated they want to build, and for which they are trying to find locations, will this last happening speed up the government in building those two new institutions that are so badly needed?

subtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN BUILDING NEW PENAL INSTITUTIONS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have been going as quickly as we can in trying to find sites. Whenever we locate them, we seem to have objections from the local communities. I might say we are going ahead on a site at Mission and another at Kamloops. I hope we can find some other sites on the Lower Mainland.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question, too, is directed to the Solicitor General. I should like to get back to the facts in the case. In this particular instance the information that a country was willing to accept the prisoners was, I understand, not conveyed to the prisoners. Can the Solicitor General tell
June 11, 1975

us why this information was not given to the prisoners holding the hostages?

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON FOR FAILING TO INFORM PRISONERS HOLDING HOSTAGES OF COUNTRY WILLING TO ACCEPT THEM
speechtext: There was no recommendation that this information should not be given to the prisoners. But we had not reached that stage. We only received an answer from the country in question late last evening. This was being discussed by the administration at British Columbia Penitentiary when the incident took place within the consultation building and everything else came to an end.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: Not good enough.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: There are provisions under that act for either an internal inquiry or for an inquiry with outside persons. We intend to pursue the one with outside persons. No final decision has yet been made but we do agree there should be such an inquiry.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON MINISTER DID NOT MAKE STATEMENT ON INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES

speechtext:
Hear, hear!

If the hon. member wishes, I have no objection to making a statement to the House and I will still make one on motions.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON MINISTER DID NOT MAKE STATEMENT ON INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: In the light of the public concern shown over this incident, a concern which is shared by members on both sides of the House, would the Prime Minister not consent to ordering an inquiry at which witnesses could be called and evidence taken under oath by a royal commission or a public inquiry under the law so that the whole thing could be aired? I ask this question in all seriousness, not only because of this tragic event but because it may trigger other events in other penitentiaries in the future if prisoners can get away with this kind of thing.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext:
On the
inquiry, Mr. Speaker, I believe the Solicitor General has answered that the government has the intention of initiating one. As for the comment about getting away with it in the future, I would point out to the hon. member that there has been a tragedy, and that a loss of life is a very regrettable thing. The first priority of the government was to make sure that the hostages would be treated safely, and that any solution that we found would not result in the kind of tragedy that occurred. There was a second priority, which was to make sure that the criminals themselves did not escape into some other country where they would go unharmed, and this was a priority that the government was determined to follow. It is only because we had that priority, too, that hopefully this kind of tragedy will not happen elsewhere, and I hope that we will have the support of the opposition on that matter.

BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would think that the Prime Minister would know where I stand, and where this party or anybody else for that matter stands on this question.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:

June 11, 1975

government actually agree to this? If so, what was the name of the country, what were the terms of that agreement, and was it ever communicated to the prisoners in question? I agree with the Prime Minister's priority that the lives of the hostages were at stake.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES

I think it is known that one of the conditions was that they would be apprehended on arrival and returned to us. subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister.
In view of the recent events in British Columbia, could the Prime Minister advise the House whether he intends to reconsider the position of his government with regard to the reinstatement of capital punishment for those found guilty of premeditated murder, so that tragedies similar to those we have witnessed in the past do not happen again in other Canadian prisons?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not going to make a statement on the British Columbia penitentiary incident, but at the request of the opposition I shall do so.
At approximately eight o'clock a.m. on June 9, 1975, three inmates of the maximum security British Columbia Penitentiary, New Westminster, British Columbia, armed with two knives, took 14 persons, including three women, hostage and forced them into a file vault of the institution's former classification building. Sole access to the vault is through a steel door.
Initially the three inmates demanded drugs and equipment to restrain the hostages. Their next demands were to see Garry Bannerman of Radio Station CKNW, Mordecai Briemberg of the Communist Party of Canada (Marxist-Leninist), and legal aid lawyers Sorachan, Williams and Jackson. The three inmates are Dwight Lucas, Andrew Graydon Bruce and Clair Daniel Wilson. Later in the day, through Briemberg and Bannerman, the inmates demanded transportation with their hostages via helicopter to Vancouver International Airport, for onward transportation to some country which has no extradition treaty with Canada.
Throughout the day the inmates maintained dialogue with prison authorities through their chosen intermediaries while holding a knife at the throat of one of the women hostages. Our principal concern at this time was to save the lives involved and to gain time.
During the evening and night of June 9/10 action was undertaken, through the Department of External Affairs, at the Solicitor General's request, to determine if some country would be willing to accept the inmates on humanitarian grounds to save the lives of the hostages. We realized that it would be virtually impossible to find a
B.C. Prison Hostages
country which would take inmates with such serious criminal records, but we wanted to make an effort to show our good faith to the inmates and convince them that their demands were unreasonable and unrealistic.
The Department of External Affairs approached several countries to accept the inmates. Most refused outright, while some took the request under consideration. Finally, late on June 10, late last night, one accepted, on condition that the inmates be incarcerated on arrival and then returned to Canada. As a result of this acceptance, initial steps were taken to establish a contingency plan which could be presented to the cabinet and then to the inmates.
However, at approximately one o'clock this morning, B.C. time, the hostages managed to get all but Mary Steinhauser and two inmates into the vault, closed the door and overpowered their remaining antagonist. The institution security force standing by and observing this action rushed the inmates holding Mary Steinhauser. In the struggle Mary Steinhauser and one inmate were seriously injured. Both were transported to hospital where Ms. Steinhauser died shortly after. The inmate is said to be in critical condition.
The exemplary conduct displayed by the hostages throughout this difficult incident and the professionalism displayed by the staff of the British Columbia penitentiary, under the regional headquarters direction, in spite of the tragic conclusion of this incident, deserve the highest commendation.
A police investigation is being conducted, and the Canadian Penitentiary Service will establish an inquiry with respect to the entire incident.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on my side of the House appreciate that the minister has been under a great deal of pressure. We are therefore grateful for the statement he has been able to make. We are exceedingly sorry to hear that a lady died in such unfortunate circumstances.
This tragedy brings to the fore the concern of Canadians for an efficient system of administration of justice. They are concerned about law and order and the protection of society. That being so, we hoped the minister would give a somewhat fuller assurance about the nature of the inquiry. Can he assure this House and country if there is to be, literally, a public inquiry? During the question period he mentioned that an inquiry would be held under the Penitentiaries Act. I do not see why it should not be an open, public inquiry. It could be held under the Penitentiaries Act, or as a royal commission.
The inquiry should not just look into the unfortunate factors which led up to the incident in the B.C. Penitentiary. It should look into the entire question of penitentiaries. Although we do not know the full facts, we do know that a report was made about a year and a half ago which recommended changes in the penitentiary administration of B.C. There was a recommendation that at least one, possibly two, new maximum security prison areas should be established.
We do not need more institutions like the one at Kamloops and Mission, which I understand are medium or intermediate security prisons. We have known for some time that inmates at New Westminster are overcrowded.

June 11, 1975
B.C. Prison Hostages
There has been a high staff turnover. The staff at New Westminster are paid less than their provincial counterparts at Okalla. Maximum security areas at New Westminster are overcrowded.
Following on this tragedy we need the assurance that there is to be a full, open inquiry, which will use this tragedy as the catalyst for focusing attention on conditions in penitentiaries. As I said, most are overcrowded, including New Westminster. I know that our priority is the safety of life, yet we must explore conditions in penitentiaries. What happened at New Westminster may make tinder boxes of other penitentiaries in this country.
Some questions need to be answered. For instance, how did such three dangerous criminals gain access to a classification area which is considered as being a relatively medium security area? After all, these were no ordinary criminals. One was an axe killer; he had killed a woman in front of her seven-year daughter. The other had stabbed a sheriff and stabbed an RCMP police officer. One of them had shot two people.
We know the minister's concern about capital punishment. I respect that concern. Much as we welcome plans to reform and rehabilitate those who are incarcerated in our penal institutions, we say that the minister, who is responsible for the administration of justice, must face the question of capital punishment and bring it back before this House.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
We must deal with that question, regardless of how we may feel as individuals. In my time as a member of this House I have seen that topic discussed on a number of occasions. Our people are concerned about our administration of justice; they are worried about permissiveness in our society, and feel frustrated because there is no opportunity for this House to debate capital punishment.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has talked about conflicting priorities. Obviously, safety of life is one priority; is it higher than the recapturing or reincarcerating of escaped criminals? We cannot adhere to a double standard. The Prime Minister likes to philosophize about respect for law and order, and then he turns round and condones an official double-cross. These questions will need to be considered.
Other questions need to be answered. For instance, after the government had asked other countries if they would accept these criminals, and after most countries had refused and one accepted, on certain conditions, why did it take the Prime Minister and cabinet five hours to discuss the situation? Why was there that time lag? Why did it take so long to get in touch with officials at the scene, and get some type of response from the inmates? During that time the situation came to such a tragic climax.
Public opinion demands a full and open inquiry into not only the New Westminster tragedy but the whole question of the administration of justice within our penitentiary service, to give full protection to those in the service on

guard over the criminals. New Westminster is not a healthy situation.
The minister still has to face the question which is causing him so much concern, and bring back to the floor of this House the fundamental question involving life, namely, capital punishment. We should have an opportunity to air that question again. It would take care of some of the public frustration. The government seems sometimes to be more concerned about perverting the law by just having commutation wholesale rather than on a selective basis.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for the statement and express to him our appreciation of the difficulties and the tensions he has been under. It is always easy to use hindsight in these kinds of things.
I think I speak for every member of this House when I say that we would like to express to the mother and sister of Mary Steinhauser, the deceased hostage, our deepest and most sincere condolences. It is somewhat ironic that the deceased hostage was well-known for her dedication to improvement of our penal institutions. She was well-known for her sympathies with those who have to work and live within them. That is a part of this tragedy that makes this a doubly sad occasion.
As I say, hindsight is always easy. However, there are some very serious questions that must be asked about this particular incident. The first question to ask is whether it is routine or why it is that three, and in this case there were four, of the most dangerous criminals in Canada are allowed into the classification area of that prison with one security guard in attendance. Each of those prisoners had a past history of desperate conduct. One recently tried to escape. All were serving life sentences, two for murder, and one for attempted murder.
It is a legitimate question to ask whether the security system in this institution and in other maximum security institutions is being administered properly by the Solicitor General's department. These are not cheap political shots. These questions have been raised over and over in this House. We would like some action in terms of security and protection for those who have to work in these institutions.
The second question that has to be resolved, and it is the reason we call for an inquiry, concerns the delay that arose between the indication that an unnamed country was willing to accept these prisoners and making the decision on when to relate the information, and the reasons given for not relating the information. I would say that cries out for a full investigation. I do not mean having a department investigate this. Frankly, that is a waste of time.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: We have had a lot of internal investigations. In this case the public are entitled to the full light of day on all of these facts. I recommend that we appoint a supreme court judge who is rich in criminal law experience, one with good common sense. We should get outside the civil service and bring someone in to have a look at this whole situation.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
June 11, 1975

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
A departmental investigation is ridiculous. It will not satisfy the public in any way, shape or form. The public have been concerned about these institutions for quite some time. It is necessary to get outside the service and see that justice is not only done but is perceived to be done.
A difficult question was posed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in answering one of the questions put to him. He said "Well, it's all right for you guys, but you are not on the spot." I recognize the government had a dilemma in terms of whether it should release three desperate and dangerous criminals. However, there is a precedent in this country, the Cross case.
No one in this party objected to the procedure followed in the Cross case. I do not know of anyone crying because the criminals in the Cross case are somewhere abroad. I believe that was the right approach. I hope the government took that approach.
I am concerned indeed that there is an ambiguity in the statements that were received today on the question of the release of those prisoners and the question of the protection of those hostages. I sincerely hope the government did not try to have it both ways in this case. That would be a case of compounding this very serious tragedy.
In view of the severe criticism the government has had over the years in terms of its penal service administration, and in view of this being one incident in many, we should not forget this tragedy. Mary Steinhauser should not have died in vain. We cannot go on playing the same game. We need a full public inquiry into the way these maximum security institutions are run.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we know what tomorrow holds in as much as it is made and influenced by the Solicitor General. Another tragedy has just occurred at New Westminster. The only answer of this government is to extend, through the Solicitor General, their sincere sympathy to the bereaved family, congratulations to those who risked their lives in spite of the minister's indolence, and finally, to order an inquiry which will remain on the shelves like all previous police investigations.
Mr. Speaker, a similar tragedy occurred not so long ago, at Cowansville, in the province of Quebec; the circumstances were different but the consequences were similar. A prison guard was killed there. The next day the minister was asked what he intended to do. Did he intend to take measures or was he taking measures to guarantee maximum security in our prisons, to protect our prison guards and encourage them to work, and particularly, to protect our society. This minister, in an eloquent and remarkable endeavour, said he extended the family his sincerest sympathy, and he had ordered an inquiry.
Mr. Speaker, this did not prevent another tragedy, at New Westminster this time. The three murderers concerned who held 14 hostages at New Westminster were well-known, hardened criminals convicted for premeditated and capital murders, and they had been sentenced to life imprisonment.
B.C. Prison Hostages
Yet, the minister should understand that those three individuals who played the heros, which cost the life of an innocent person were already under the maximum penalty before taking the hostages, namely life imprisonment. Neither do they fear, regardless of the seriousness of their crimes, a more severe penalty because even before the tragedy at Cowansville, before the tragedy at New Westminster, those criminals had already been condemned, before they did anything, to the maximum penalty provided under the act, regardless of the seriousness of their murder, that is life emprisonment.
Proceeding from that principle rejected by the minister-and he is staking his political life on it-it does not matter to the inmate whether he kills one, two or five prison guards with whatever weapon he can use to commit another crime, a knife, a revolver or other weapon, his penalty will not be any more severe than before his crime. He is already under the maximum penalty.
Mr. Speaker, this is how happen deplorable and absolutely unfortunate situations such as we have just witnessed at New Westminster, when we have to find an obliging country ready to assume towards the criminals the responsibilities which we have failed to accept.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I suggest that the minister will be held directly responsible of those tragedies so long as he refuses to allow the House to review the matter of capital punishment and to reinstate it in cases of premeditated murder.
Mr. Speaker, as reported in Hansard for May 5, on page 5452, the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Papros-ki) asked the following question: Will the government consider a national referendum on the abolition or retention of capital punishment? The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) replied: The government has no such intention. When the hon. member for Edmonton Centre asked for a national referendum with a view to ascertaining public opinion on the matter, the President of the Privy Council answered:
Mr. Speaker, at every general election, the people of this country have some imput. The last time they elected a majority of Liberals.
There is the government' answer and the manner,-in between tragedies-it considers the problem. So, when there is no tragedy, the government refuses to consider the issue of capital punishment, refuses to reconsider it, when it knows that public opinion is very much divided on the issue and disappointed by the administration of justice at present.
When an unfortunate tragedy occurs, everybody agrees. Then, the minister makes a fine statement or extends his sympathy. But, Mr. Speaker, tomorrow another tragedy could take place and there is absolutely no guarantee that measures are being taken by the department, since, for the government, it is a purely political issue. I think, and I know this is a serious charge, that the minister's own head or department are more important to him than the protection of innocent human lives in prisons. That is why I think I am expressing the views of many of my fellow-citizens when I say I am deeply disappointed to see that such murders, such crimes can be committed in an organized and civilized society with impunity.

June 11, 1975
B.C. Prison Hostages

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: Order. I appreciate, of course, the circumstances in which the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) changed his mind about making a statement on motions, but this does not take away from the fact that the Chair has already allowed a number of questions on this subject today. Had the Chair known then that a statement on motions would be made, and that there would have been an opportunity to ask questions later, the Chair would not have shown the latitude it did. In the circumstances I think hon. members ought to be quite brief in their questions. The subject has been well ventilated. I shall try not to restrict questions too severely, but I think we ought to come quickly to the point.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
have a question for the Solicitor General, Mr. Speaker. I ask him this question fully realizing that it is after the event and recognizing, also, the pressure under which he and the government were living yesterday. But we need a little more light, I think, on what happened during the five hours between the receipt of the information that a country was prepared to accept these criminals and the final confrontation at the penitentiary. Was there, in fact, a decision taken by the government in the course of those five hours that this offer would not be accepted but that this would not be communicated to the criminals in question because, as I understand it, there was no communication of any aspect of this offer to the criminals?
Was there in fact a decision taken not to act on this offer or, on the other hand, was it the case that in the course of those five hours, to put it dramatically, with a woman with a knife to her throat, the government was unable to reach a decision as to what it should do?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
To begin with, I am not sure whether it was five hours. I was at the telephones for more than 24 hours-I know it was a long time. But as soon as I was advised that the country in question would accept the prisoners under certain conditions, I immediately consulted with my deputy minister, the Commissioner of Penitentiaries, and some other senior people in the department. That took maybe half an hour or 45 minutes. I then got in touch with the Prime Minister and discussed it with him.
I then immediately called British Columbia to speak to the regional director. He had spent the whole night there the night before and he had gone home for the first time in two days. I could not get him at the penitentiary, but finally I got him at his home in Abottsford. I discussed the matter with him, described the offer as conveyed to me by the Department of External Affairs and asked him to think about the implications, discuss them with the leading people in the B.C. region, and call me back as soon as possible.
I told him that among the issues we had to resolve were whether he thought there was any chance of the offer being accepted by the inmates, and who should convey the offer to the inmates if we were to convey it. I wanted his advice on how we were to carry it out, and how quickly. I wanted his advice on the particular offer. He said he would do that. He returned to the penitentiary after he

had freshened up a bit. He went back to New Westminster. I was waiting for his call.
We called him later, and he said they were getting further reports on the situation inside the place where the hostages were, and that everything seemed cool and calm and most people were going to settle down for the night. He said he would be discussing the offer from the foreign country shortly and that he would call me back. I waited. The next thing that happened was that I got a call indicating that the hostages inside had tried to overcome their captors.
Both the hostages and the inmates inside the classification wing knew we had asked several countries for permission to send them there. When we had received answers from those countries, and most of the answers were no, we would report as soon as possible to the inmates saying we were waiting for others, and so on. They knew there were certain outstanding responses to come in. Before a final assessment of that offer was received, this further incident occurred where a girl was killed.
With respect to the fact that the girl was killed, I must say that throughout the entire period one of the inmates was holding a knife to the throat of one girl or other. They used that as a means of controlling the other 13 hostages since there were only three inmates and 14 captives.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: I do not want to be unfair about it and I do not want to be critical of any individuals, but I should like to ask the Solicitor General this question: in view of the lapse of time, whether five hours or four and a half hours, and the obvious pressure and fatigue for the people on the spot with responsibility, does the Solicitor General honestly feel that the government's apparatus and organization for dealing with this kind of emergency are adequate? I ask that question in view, as I say, of the fatigue obviously involved for the limited number of people associated with this operation, the difficulty of getting word back and forth, and of making a decision in a great emergency.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I say, as soon as the message was received we did nothing else but work on this particular offer. We wanted to make sure that the offer would not be misunderstood and that it would be conveyed properly. As I say, we wanted the advice of the people on the spot. At one time we considered whether we should send the offer directly into the inmates, but that was advised against because of the tenseness of the situation there, and I took the advice of the people on the spot.
There was no sitting around or delay. There were discussions, many telephone conversations. It so happened that when we tried to get the regional director, for the first time in a long period he had just gone home to change and freshen up. I am not sure how far Abbotsford is from New Westminster, but he had gone home. He got dressed immediately and returned to the penitentiary.
It was understood by nearly everyone that at a certain period of the day they would not hear anything else during that day, and that they would wait until the morning for further answers to come in on the request made to
June 11, 1975

the different countries. Everyone had the impression that everything was all right and that there was no great pressure at that time. For one reason or other the hostages decided at a given point that they were going to overcome their captors, and of course that led to the situation where a person died. They were no doubt acting in the best of faith. They were frightened. They knew the offers were out. But as I say, there was no delay. We were given the impression that there was no time limit, that everyone was willing to wait till morning since night time had come.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the minister advise the House, not of the last time that the communication was received in terms of the country that was apparently willing to take these prisoners, but of the last time a communication was given to the prisoners and hostages concerning the level of activity in regard to meeting the demands of the prisoners? At what time were they last advised as to the progress of the negotiations?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
It is hard for me to say, Mr. Speaker. As I said, I made many, many telephone calls. I think on Monday night as soon as I got to sleep the phone rang again, and I had no sleep at all that night. Last night I think I was in bed for about two hours, so I forget.
I know I phoned many times to British Columbia. I dealt with three people-the regional director, the acting regional director, and the director of the penitentiary. I had many conversations with these three individuals and they worked with the team that was discussing matters with the inmates and hostages. I had one conversation with Mr. Bannerman on Monday. I conveyed information as quickly as I could, and they conveyed it to me as quickly as they could. I was dealing back and forth with Ottawa as well.
I was lucky, Mr. Speaker, because we had gone to Toronto for a conference. We did not attend the conference at all, but as a result I had my senior people right with me at my hotel and throughout the whole night we were together and in consultation.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate the difficulties inherent in this kind of situation, but would the minister advise whether the condition of the hostages themselves prior to this unfortunate incident was assessed by anybody on the scene? These hostages had been held since approximately eight o'clock on Monday. The final incident apparently took place at one o'clock western time last night. Did anyone assess the physical or mental conditions of the hostages as well as of the prisoners? Obviously the prime concern would be to see that no precipitate action took place on the part of the prisoners. What kind of assessment took place regarding the risks inherent in keeping that many people enclosed over that period of time?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had a report late yesterday, I think late in the evening eastern time, perhaps around midnight. I was told that that would be eight or nine o'clock in the west, but I cannot be sure of the exact time. I was told they had ordered supper for all the inmates and hostages from outside, and that everything seemed to be as well as possible under the circumstances, that everyone appeared cool.
B.C. Prison Hostages
By the way, the penitentiary employees outside the classification unit could see inside, and on one occasion they brought out hostages so they could be seen by the people outside, and they seemed to be well. The negotiating team also said they seemed to be well. The conditions were not the best, but there was no hysteria or undue concern shown by the hostages. They seemed very cool and placid considering it was a very difficult situation. So the assessment was that in the circumstances things were pretty calm and under control, in the sense of control in these circumstances.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: As a final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, is the minister satisfied that the action that precipitated the unfortunate struggle in this incident was on the side of the hostages, or was it on the side of the inmates? Is there any indication at this point as to the causal factor of the struggle that took place?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: I am advised that the hostages at a given point decided that they would try and overcome their captors, the inmates. What led them to decide at that particular time to act one does not know, but they did act all of a sudden. Again I understand that one of the inmates had been given drugs. He was a drug addict and drugs were given him because it was felt that by supplying the drugs he might fall asleep or become high; and in fact that is what happened to him. He became high on drugs and he was easy to overcome. I guess that at a given time they thought they could take action, they picked up a tripod and went after the other inmates. A struggle ensued and the guards came in, and shots were fired. We still do not know the exact cause of death of the girl who died, Mary Steinhauser; that will be assessed and we will be getting a medical report.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I just ask one question. At what time was it that the authorities in British Columbia became aware of the fact that the hostages intended to try to overcome the inmates?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
This came without warning, Mr. Speaker. I was told by the regional director that they were in their offices, actually discussing the proposal from the country I mentioned earlier, and they had just started their discussions when they heard the shots fired and they rushed out. By the time they got there they were bringing out the bodies and so on.
The correctional officers at the institution were outside this special classification unit. They were watching and waiting, and their instructions were not to invade the unit unless harm was being done to the hostages or unless a struggle ensued. As soon as they saw a struggle under way they went in and tried to save as many lives as possible and reduce the conflict.

June 11, 1975
B.C. Prison Hostages

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just two questions for the minister and I will ask them both at once. As the minister remembers, back in 1973 we had a major problem in the British Columbia Penitentiary with a riot. At that time a motion that I put forward in this House was passed, setting up a committee of this House to investigate security at penitentiaries. I should like to know whatever happened to that report because it seems now we are going to set up another committee, and two years from now there will not be anything done in respect of that penitentiary.
Secondly, the minister said in one of his answers today that they were building penitentiaries in Kamloops and Mission. I think the minister is aware that neither of those is to be a maximum security institution. The city of Lilloo-et has offered a location to the federal government, and the minister said they had turned it down a number of times. In fact the city of Lillooet is begging for the federal government to build a maximum security penitentiary there, and I wonder if the minister could advise us if they are going to go ahead with that maximum security institution. It certainly would be a good place for animals of the type that were in that room last night, the three of them, to be sent to, because you have to segregate those people from the other ones who are in that institution, or you are going to continue to have those problems.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
I would agree; we are actively examining the Lillooet site, and a decision will be made shortly. I think I should also point out that we looked at a site in the hon. member's riding and the people there did not want that particular site. It is a difficult thing, especially in populated areas, to find public acceptance for a maximum security penitentiary.
In respect of the other question regarding the committee that was set up in the last parliament, if you will recall, a special sub-committee of the justice committee was set up to study security and other matters in the penitentiary services following a series of escapes and other problems in the penitentiaries. That committee was under the chairmanship of the present Assistant Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole House, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin).
They carried on work in different parts of the country, but they were unable to get the committee together for a report. As a result, the hon. lady chairman sent me an individual report of her own. Some other members of the committee sent me their individual reports, but other members did not. There was never a report of the entire committee. I had the benefit of those personal reports, but there was never a report tabled by the committee.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order, or perhaps a question of privilege. The minister stated that the commission came into my riding and looked for a site to build a penitentiary but the people of my riding turned it down. I think that is misleading the House to a great

extent. They wanted to put it at a certain location in my riding, which the people would not accept. The people of my riding proposed other locations in the riding that would be quite acceptable. The location we are talking about is in the middle of a residential area where there is also an airport. I think the minister should withdraw that point as it is very unfair to say that the people of my riding turned down a penitentiary in the riding. They turned down the location which, to the majority of my people, including a former Liberal member, is a poor location.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEATH OF WOMAN HOSTAGE AT B.C. PENITENTIARY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was federal government property, formerly a military base, and it was assessed as being a good site. I just say to the hon. member that the people in the area did not want a penitentiary on that site, and perhaps there were good reasons. I am not aware of the other sites in the riding to which he referred, but we would be glad to look at them.

speechtext:
1.	Was the Department of Supply and Services directed by Treasury Board to develop an efficient and effective EDP procurement organization to service all departments and agencies?
2.	What has been the progress to date?
3.	How many independent EDP groups do work for the Department?
4.	Where do the responsibilities of these respective groups lie in terms of the many departments and agencies in government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Minister of Supply and Services):
subsubtopic: EDP PROCUREMENT
speechtext:
1. Yes, except in those circumstances where DSS considers delegation of purchasing authority to departments or agencies to be more effective.
2.	The Department of Supply and Services received TB approval on September 21, 1973 to establish an EDP organization which would plan and consolidate the procurement of all EDP goods and services in accordance with Treasury Board Circular Letter 1972-24 relating to EDP in the federal government. Its reorganized Electronics and Data Processing Sector has consolidated the procurement of EDP goods and services for some 60 user departments and agencies. Beneficial bulk procurement arrangements have been brought about for items in common use, as have improvements in the services available to users and in the efficiency with which procurement resources are used. In the fiscal year 1973-74 contracts were issued with a total value of $81 millions, and the estimated value for 1974-75 is $100 millions.
3.	In DSS: There are three EDP responsibility centres. In the Private Sector: There are 480 independent EDP groups or companies to date on our source lists, of which some 350 have received DSS contracts.
4.	DSS: (a) The first group is the procurement organization within the Electronics and Data Processing Sector which arranges all contracting for EDP goods and services, (b) The second group operates computer-aided text processing equipment as part of the system for printing government publications, including Hansard, (c) The Services Administration of DSS maintains a computer network for pay and related matters. Private Sector: The private sector provides hardware, software and services under contract to DSS in satisfaction of requisitions received by DSS from government departments and agencies.

subsubtopic: EDP EQUIPMENT
speechtext:

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this amendment to Bill C-50 I should give special consideration to the opportunities for agricultural production that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is overlooking. If there ever was an opportunity in this country or this world for the production of food we have that opportunity now in Canada. We have the producers who are ready, willing, and waiting to produce food for a hungry world.
One of the problems we have to deal with exists because we have a Minister of Agriculture who lacks imagination and apparently the initiative to legislate programs which would be not only to the benefit of the producers, but ultimately to the benefit of the consumers in Canada and to the population of a hungry world. To me it is immoral to limit the production of food.
We have to exercise care that we do not enter into or negotiate those types of legislation that will limit food production. We have to exercise great care primarily because we are an agricultural oriented country. The urbanization of Canada is increasing very rapidly. Up to the present time a great many urban dwellers who are also consumers have more or less left administration policy to those who are interested in the production of food. This is good, providing the proper climate is established or is in evidence for ultimate production. I think it is incumbent on each and every one of us in this House of Commons to ensure that this comes about.
It is very difficult, especially for those of us in the opposition, to get the Minister of Agriculture to accept those policies which are not only going to be to the benefit of the producers but also the benefit of consumers.
I realize that stabilization was enacted in an effort to get away from the boom and bust cycle. This is all right so far as the majority of producers are concerned. However, what is unacceptable to them is that if they had to take a lower average income because of stabilization than they would have as an over-all average in the boom and bust cycle, this would be to the detriment of agriculture. This is why we must exercise a great deal of care in initiating policies for the benefit of Canadians. I am sure this is one reason why this matter concerned so many people in committee, and interested so many people across Canada.
Many representations were made to the committee. Surely it is not necessary for me to remind the minister that members of the opposition on the committee had to fight very hard indeed for the right of witnesses to appear
Agricultural Stabilization Act
before the committee, and for representations to be made. A large number of groups and organizations are vitally concerned about this legislation, not the least of whom is the minister of agriculture for the province of Ontario. I realize I shall not be able to cover all the points I consider important in respect of this legislation, but my colleagues during the course of this afternoon and during future sessions when this legislation is being debated I am sure will bring these other points to the attention of the House.
I wish to read into the record certain statements made by the minister of agriculture for the province of Ontario. He said:
Bill C-50 represents a most significant piece of agricultural legislation. Its importance has been emphasized by the representations made to the standing committee by various farm organizations. The problems inherent in deriving an effective income protection program are many; the regional make-up of our country, the numerous commodities to be considered, the constitutional framework of the country, that is, who should assume the responsibility or be involved in a stabilization plan-the federal and/or provincial governments and/or farmers.
Then he went on to state further:
First, we believe the federal government has an obligation to place a floor on farm prices that prevents the kind of disaster prices that drive farmers from the land. We suggest that the federal government guarantee a price at 90 per cent of the average price for the last five years, and more preferably the last three years. The federal government would make a payment to all producers when the price fell below that level.
Many people are concerned that this bill could give a great deal of power to the Minister of Agriculture and the government without imposing any obligation on them. It would seem that the minister has it both ways. This is not good enough when one considers the past record of the minister. He has moved about the country telling the urban people, the consumers, that they will have to pay more for the products they use on their tables. I am sure everyone understands this when one considers the tremendous amount of good land that is being gobbled up by the large cities.
If I remember the figures correctly, I believe in the province of Ontario something in the order of 20 acres go out of production every hour. A similar situation exists in western Canada where the cities are alsd growing. With good agricultural land being taken out of production I am sure the time is not too distant when the Minister of Agriculture will have an obligation to encourage producers to produce to the fullest of their capability.
One concern we have about this legislation is that, if at any stage the minister decided that the producers were producing too much in any aspect of agriculture, he could place curbs on production to the detriment not only of the producers of the product but ultimately the consumer.
In referring to the portion of the bill that this amendment would delete I wish to mention two lines:
For the purpose of stabilizing the price of an agricultural commodity, the Board may exercise such other powers as are prescribed by the Governor in Council...
That would give tremendous power to the Minister of Agriculture. I do not think this is desirable. Nor do I believe it is for the benefit of the producers. If it is not for the benefit of the producers then ultimately it certainly will not be for the benefit of the consumers. If there should be a shortage due to the shortcomings of any policy

June 11, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
of the government, then ultimately the consumers will suffer.
I should like to place on the record a statement made by the Canadian Pork Council. At page 2 of the brief presented by this council we find the following:
The interim stabilization plan was developed on the concept of the federal government guaranteeing a margin of $22.41 per hundredweight over a nationally weighted average feed cost.
The feed cost was developed from two basic feed formuli-one using western grain, the other basically a corn ration. The national average feed cost is of course weighted by the preponderance of feed usage in eastern Canada. The amount of grain used in the former was 548 pounds per hog with a protein level of 13 per cent-both of which are considered by the pork council to be unrealistically low. Not only was the five year "cost" inadequate in that it contained too little feed and protein, but moreover did not include other costs of production.
Surely it is not necessary for me to remind the minister that in committee and during the debate on second reading I, and my colleagues on this side of the House, wished the minister to include in the cost of production transportation costs to market. He apparently is of the opinion that this would be difficult to do. Surely with all the computer systems available in Canada it would not be too difficult to provide a little equality between eastern and western Canada, or vice-versa.
This brief further states:
The margin was struck as the difference between the nationally weighted price and the nationally weighted feed cost, and is guaranteed at 90 per cent. The effective support level is about $42 per hundred (the cumulative feed grain cost from April 1, 1974 to February 1, 1975 was $20.64).
At the level of $42 per hundredweight the support for 1974 was found to be so low, compared to current costs, that all provinces, with the exception of Ontario and Manitoba, provided for some level of market price assistance for varying periods of time during 1974. In Manitoba a payment to sustain and encourage production was made to producers for the increase in their production this year over last year.
That is the problem with which this bill should be dealing. I am disappointed that the Minister of Agriculture has not initiated a program which, as I said earlier, would benefit the producers and ultimately the consumers. In his position as minister he would be capable of bringing in such a program. I think that he has reneged on his responsibilities because he has not established such a policy in agreement with the provinces, a policy which would be for the benefit of the producers. It is not good enough for him to bring in this type of program, and take credit for it even though it does not work. He can then go on the hustings and say to the electors that he brought in Bill C-50, the stabilization program. That is not good enough, because a program that is to benefit the producers and ultimately the consumers must work.
Let me quote some more of the statements contained in the brief of the Canadian Pork Council. This is what they said:
On the marketing side there is no single national market for pork. There are a series of provincial or regional markets with the Ontario market being the major one. For the most part all other markets are priced below the Toronto market. One of the major concerns of the Pork Council members during the past year, particularly the western members, has been the price discrepancies which exist between their markets and the Toronto market. The difference has been usually much wider than the cost of moving pork into eastern markets. For example, as can be seen from the attached appendix, the price spread

between Saskatoon and Toronto for 1974 was $7.66 per cwt. This is slightly more than $4 per cwt. more than the cost of trucking pork from Saskatoon to Toronto even at the new 1975 rates. Saying so however, the council does recognize that ready availability of supplies is in some situations and circumstances worth some level of premium.
We have to recognize that agricultural organizations, producers, provincial governments and their agricultural committees are concerned.
The Pork Council submission goes on to read:
However, as noted, the Pork Council believes that programs to assure at least minimum income should be the responsibility of the federal government and therefore we believe that a federal stabilization program should be tailored to serve regional needs and thus deal with all producers and regions comparably. In our view the establishment of a federal program with different regional applications, if circumstances dictate the need of it, is far preferable to a series of competitive provincial agreements "top loaded" on a basic national program. This is precisely the kind of program that pork producers have experienced during the past year, and which they have been looking forward to getting out of and into a national plan financed by the federal government.
This is exactly what I have been talking about. No doubt my colleagues will be discussing this further. The federal government has shortchanged the producers of Canada by not initiating this type of program which will ultimately benefit the producers, stabilize the agricultural industry, and benefit the consumers. I see that you are ready to rise, Mr. Speaker, to remind me that my time is up. I thank you for your consideration.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to explain just why I felt it necessary to put this amendment before the House. In my view it is a sad day when we are ready to grant more and more power to the government which it does not know how to use. Yet it wants absolute power. The clause which I propose be deleted from the bill grants this power to the government.
Whatever powers the minister or the government can devise between now and kingdom come can be used by the minister and the Department of Agriculture under this bill. He does not have to come back to parliament to ask for more power because, for instance, there is a problem which might arise in some parts of Canada; he can go ahead and solve it without parliament. To many who do not treasure democracy and who do not believe in representative government, this may be the way things should be done. Although representative government may not be the most efficient form of government, it is still the best there is. Some people may say that granting such powers to the government may make it more efficient and may make civil servants more authoritative. This is what this clause is doing.
The present Agricultural Stabilization Act which this clause amends contains a clause dealing with powers. I am referring to clause 7 (a) to (g), which deals with specific powers that the government can use to implement or stabilize the prices of agricultural commodities. The minister said that was not enough, he wanted more powers. The hon. member who spoke before me said that more power might be all right but that under our federal system there should have been further consultations with provincial governments regarding what powers they would approve. This is also my view.
June 11, 1975

I have a letter here, written by a young person in Virden, Manitoba, saying that the people over there do not quite understand the Minister of Agriculture and they would like me to attempt to explain my views to them. I attempted to do this to my constituents, but I hesitate to write to Virden, Manitoba. In explaining my objections to this clause I stated the following in the House on October 15:
There are two basic directions we can take to tackle our mounting problems; one is socialistic, with state participation in all sectors, and the other is through a free market economy with over-all state control.
In this way the economy can be gauged and we know exactly where it is at. Most members of the old Liberal party would have had no objection to taking any of those two directions, and no objections to going along with a free market economy and over-all state control. But this Liberal government and the Minister of Agriculture do not feel that is enough. They want to tinker with society and they want state participation in all sectors of society. That is spelled out in the two agricultural bills before the House, Bill C-41 which deals with grain for export, and Bill C-50 which deals with every other agricultural commodity produced except for western grain, which is being dealt with under Bill C-41.
The deputy minister of agriculture spoke before the Committee on Agriculture with regard to Bill C-41. He said we have two bills under study. I should like to quote him from page 44 of Committee Proceedings 41. He said that Bill C-41 is designed to deal with western grains, the six major grains. He went on to say that 70 per cent of that production is for export. Then he said:
-I think you have the two bills before you. Indeed at one point, it was even considered calling the western bill an export and market insurance bill because that was the heavy orientation of it. However, it is still called the Western Grain Stabilization Act, but that is the primary difference that we see here.
The difference is that this bill deals with commodities produced in Canda and most of that production which is marketed in Canada. I have a growing fear that in granting the government a blank cheque or powers beyond what the minister has today, it will turn to supply management. The minister of agriculture of the province of Ontario also had this fear which he voiced during his appearance before the committee. He said:
Under 10(1) (1.1) of Bill C-50 our interpretation of the wording "may exercise such other powers as are prescribed by the Governor in Council for that purpose" to mean the possibility of production controls or supply management.
I share that fear, Mr. Speaker. Supply management is often spoken of as a goal, a dream, but to my mind it would eventually limit production to the known market for nearly every commodity produced in Canada outside of the six major grains. That known market is Canada itself. The Minister of Agriculture is a much quoted proponent of supply management and of marketing boards. It is my fear that the powers in this clause would limit production of hogs, cattle, poultry, wool, sheep, bees, honey or what have you, to be known market, that being our own consumption.
I see a world suffering from great shortages of food. I see farmers with a great desire to produce. I see over-zeal-
Agricultural Stabilization Act
ous ministers attempting to control production, supposedly so that they can get better management of it. This is particularly true when world prices are falling.
Committee proceedings No. 40 show that there were several attempts to get the minister to explain what he meant by the term "supply management". As reported at page 31 the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) posed the following question:
Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. I would just like to follow up somewhat on Mr. Horner's statement in regard to the minister's control over the agriculture sector once again. If I might quote what he stated in regard to the second reading of this bill, he stated that:
None of these programs-
He is speaking about second reading of this bill when the minister stated in this House that:
None of these programs can work without proper supply management.
The Minister's answer appears on the same page. I will not read it all, but he said:
Proper supply management means producing a commodity for a market in such a way that you know where it is going to be as much as possible.
That really means only Canada. Then, to make it abundantly clear, the hon. member for Pembina asked this question:
When this bill becomes a reality, our markets will still somewhat reflect the prices that are in the United States, will they not?
That is an innocent question, Mr. Speaker, one normally applicable to the cattle industry in western Canada. The minister replied:
The world markets for world commodities, yes, I think they reflect it much too much, as far as I am concerned, because I do not think we should be so dependent on their marketing.
He is referring to the fact that our cattle market reflects the prices of the United States market and he does not believe that we should depend on that as much as we do. That is a mighty heavy answer to give to any thinking man in the cattle industry, particularly in western Canada. How anybody could be in the cattle industry and say that we should not be concerned about prices in the United States is hard to understand. Only one who believes in rigid supply management control could make such a statement.
Since 1947 the cattle industry in western Canada has hinged on markets in the United States. During the war the border and the markets were closed, but after 1947-48 the embargo was lifted. As a result cattle prices increased by about 15 cents per pound, and we benefited from being able to ship cattle to the United States. There have been times when we suffered, but by and large we should recognize the advantage of having a market of some 240 million people available to us. This allows us to increase production and improve our efficiency and thus lower the cost of food to the Canadian consumer.
If one were to over simplify the case one could compare it to the automotive pact, the accessibility to the American market and the opportunity to increase our production and thus increase efficiency and lower the cost of cars. The sad part is that the price of cars was lowered in the United States but not in Canada. That has not happened in the beef industry in Canada.

June 11, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
One could say that beef is not a world commodity. What did the minister mean when he said "world markets for world commodities"? One could take the narrow view that beef is not a world commodity, but the evidence is that it is a world commodity and our producers suffer from world competition. If beef prices have risen in the last month or so it could be because the production of fat cattle is down in both Canada and the United States. If we had not had the recent scandal in Montreal we might have expected beef prices to rise had we not been on a world market. The production of beef in Australia is twice our production, and the amount of their production which is surplus is four times or more what our surplus has been in the last two or three years. For some time to come Australian beef exports to Canada will stop beef prices in this country from reaching prohibitive levels. The minister cannot convince me that beef is not a world commodity.
What other powers is the minister seeking? In committee I raised the subject of hogs, and the minister spoke at length about hogs. I asked if the minister intends to set up a single desk marketing system for hogs, the words "single desk" being synonymous with "marketing board" but not carrying the connotations which antagonize some people. Some people just do not like marketing boards. I wanted to know what other powers the minister wants which are not set out in subparagraphs (a), (b), (c) and (g) of subsection 10.1(2) of the stabilization bill.
In the minister's view, a single desk marketing system would stop the provinces from competing with one another. He will have a hard time convincing the hog producers of Alberta that they are not competing with hog producers of British Columbia, or the cattle producers of Alberta that they are not competing with the cattle producers of British Columbia. British Columbia produces less beef than it needs, and its hog production is somewhat deficient. Alberta hogs are sold on the Vancouver market. Therefore Alberta hogs compete directly with B.C. produced hogs.
It is not likely that the minister can use his powers to lessen competition between provinces. I have suggested that the single desk marketing system will attempt to reduce competition in hog marketing. Let us examine that idea.
At present Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba have established marketing programs under which they sell hogs to Japan. The programs are not similar and the provinces are competing with one another. As an Albertan, I am not worried about Alberta's ability to compete on the Japanese market. We can compete in hogs and in any other commodity. Apparently competition worries the minister. I do not think he is worried so much about competition between Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba; he is worried about competition between Saskatchewan and Ontario, and I suggest that the single desk marketing system, which is another name for a national marketing board, is designed to lessen that competition.
The minister does not want Saskatchewan to increase its production of hogs or cattle. The Saskatchewan farmer will be told, "We are giving you grain insurance; keep your granaries filled and, if necessary, we will make you a

payment if we fail to sell the grain. In the meantime you need not keep hogs and upset the Ontario market." That is the story they will be told.
What does the record show? In the period 1969-70 Saskatchewan increased hog production by some 70 per cent. Then when grain started to sell at high prices about a year and a half ago, Saskatchewan hog production declined by some 28 per cent. Mr. Speaker, supporters of supply management do not like such large swings in production. That is exactly what the minister suggested when answering the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) on May 20, 1975. He said, as recorded on page 40:31 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Agriculture:
Proper supply management means producing a commodity for a market in such a way that you know where it is going to be as much as possible.
Traditionally western Canada has exported 10 per cent of its hog production. Saskatchewan exports about 10 per cent of its production to the United States, and we think we can continue to do this for some time to come. We are not afraid of competition. We can compete with United States hog producers, and have proved our ability so to do.
Ontario is relatively self-sufficient in hog production and exports certain types of hogs to the United States. Quebec is also a surplus producer of hogs; it exports some of its production to Ontario and sends certain cuts to the United States. But western Canada produces feed grain, a raw commodity which is used in the manufacture of meat, if one can consider the transformation of feed grain into meat as a manufacturing process. We think we can produce more meat every year and provide more employment for Canadians in western Canada.
As I say, we consider feed grain as a raw material. I therefore see the government's two agricultural bills and the minister's support of supply management as constituting an attempt to curtail the growth of a budding agricultural manufacturing industry, as I consider the process by which we change feed grains into meat as a manufacturing process. I therefore fear the wide powers which this bill will give the minister.
In the language of the bill, the "Board may exercise such other powers as are prescribed by the Governor in Council . .." That, really, is jargon which makes the clause read better. Of course the ultimate decision still rests with the Minister of Agriculture, and that is what I fear. We know that the Governor in Council means the cabinet; therefore since the cabinet appoints the board, the cabinet will have a great say in what the board decides.
Why do I say I am afraid? In the past six or seven years we have seen a tremendous shift in the Liberal party's philosophy, a shift away from belief in the individual and a shift toward government involvement in the individual's business. The Liberal party thinks that the government should interfere as much as possible in the individual's business and no longer be content to play the part of referee.
Quite possibly the amendment before the House will be defeated and the bill may pass this afternoon. If it does there will be no need for more agricultural legislation. Legislation in the field of agriculture will become un-
June 11, 1975

necessary, as this can all be done by way of regulations of some board, with the approval of the minister, of course.
That is not to say there will never be another piece of legislation. Politicians, being the animals they are, they will sometimes be in doubt as to what they should do and there will be talk of legislation in the Speech from the Throne. Speeches from the Throne in the years ahead will read, "And there will be efforts in the agricultural field to deal with the problems of marketing", or something like that.
The only time there will be debates on agriculture in this House of Commons will be on debates on the Speech from the Throne, or when a minister bringing down a budget makes some adjustment in the excise taxes on agricultural commodities or increases taxes on the agricultural industry in Canada. Then there will be debates on agriculture.
Perhaps it could be said that the member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) brought all this on himself. The member for Crowfoot has often been blamed for holding up a piece of agricultural legislation for two years. The government is using this request for power as a way to ensure that will never happen again. I guess it is right.
I could not let this time in the history of Canada go by without clearly pointing out that this is fully noticed. The opposition is fully cognizant of the fact that this reach for power is one more bitter pill to swallow. It is one more loss of what I believe is representative government, a little more loss in our basic freedom, the right to speak out. The right to debate and legislate is part of our true democracy. The government is taking away that right by reaching for all the power this minister might want.
I could say to that person in Virden, Manitoba, who wrote asking what the minister is really like, that he is a nice friendly fellow, but he is being led around by an evil cabinet. To make sure he is led properly, they appointed an accountant, who knows nothing about agriculture, as his deputy minister. This minister does not know enough about agriculture to realize what is going on and what the cabinet is doing to him. He does not know enough about democracy to realize that.
I hope before this minister's political career is over he, like many Liberals before him, will realize what this cabinet is doing to him and will leave that political party. Many Liberals before him have done just that. I will not list them this afternoon. One of them was the deputy premier since 1968. He left because he saw his freedom and that of Canadian citizens escaping little by little, just as is happening this afternoon. Another minister from the province of Quebec left this cabinet. I hope I am around long enough to see the present Minister of Agriculture realize what kind of a cabinet this is.
The minister told the committee that in this particular clause, the cabinet was giving him a blank cheque. That is what he said. I could quote it from the committee proceedings. It may be giving him a blank cheque, but it is costing Canadian farmers and our agricultural industry more than money. It is costing our freedom and our ability to be flexible in production, something which has kept our agricultural industry flourishing up to this time. I hope
