Agricultural Stabilization Act
The hon. member talks about world commodity markets. Let him consider what is happening in world commodity markets because we do not just trade in beef in competition with the United States of America. We trade in competition with Argentina, Australia and New Zealand. These countries are affected. You could buy beef in Australia a little while ago for about 2 or 3 cents a pound on the hoof running around the range; all they have to do there is to leave them outside until they think the market is going to get a little better. That is the kind of market in which we compete.
I can tell the hon. member that if he wants to see the files of letters I get from western people, I get hundreds of letters from western people, some of them quite large operators. By the very action of the cattlemen in British Columbia they have accepted, by a vote of 2 to 1, a form of guarantee of security. I am sure most members of this House would have said a year ago they would not have accepted that kind of form of guarantee proposed by the government of British Columbia or by any other government. I may say I have some reservations about the program they have put into effect in British Columbia. But the fact is, the cattlemen have accepted it. It is not compulsory. It is voluntary. The cattlemen, at the annual meeting of the B.C. Cattlemen's Association, accepted it.
The hon. member talks about supply management. Let us talk about the old bill. What did it do? I am talking about the bill initiated by the former government, that tremendous bill which provided for a form of security, a bill which was readily available, the bill which was brought into the House on January 24, 1958, given third reading on January 25 and Royal Assent on January 31, 1958-it was all that quick. It was so important it all had to be done in that time.
What did that bill seek to do? They called it supply management. Under that bill, and under former governments and former ministers of agriculture, they limited the amount of money paid. For instance, on hogs they never paid on more than 200 hogs that a producer had. Under our program last year it was up to 1,500 hogs per producer. Who was limiting supply? Was it this Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan)?
Surely to God no one in the country is going to suggest to me that what is happening in the hog industry today is good. There w'as no sort of security offered for them. The hon. member for Crowfoot says: Sure, they went down in price in Saskatchewan, and production was down there because they could sell grain. He says production declined by 20 per cent. Mr. Speaker, in Saskatchewan they have the best support program, but because it was provincial and the producers know these commodities are marketed world-wide, their production went down 40 per cent. Over the whole nation the production went down 20 per cent. Is this what we want? I do not want it for the producers and I don't want it for the consumers either, because the price of pork in the last few days has been the highest ever on record in Canada.
The same thing has been happening in the United States, the same thing has happened in Italy, the same thing has happened in New Zealand. There are too many people chasing too few porkers around, that is what it

amounts to. They are all bidding for that commodity, and it is going to hurt the purchasing power in the hands of consumers. It is going to hurt the industry too, because people will discontinue using that product. That is what will happen, because there isn't enough supply to go around. Pork producers in the nation enjoyed no security because there was no program in operation.
The hon. member for Crowfoot suggests I am going to have a wondrous selling program for hogs. I think it is a very good idea, but as I say, it is up to the pork producers to adopt that kind of a program themselves. We hear it suggested by some ministers of agriculture in Canada today that the thing to do is copy the Wheat Board, make a commitment, appoint members by the government, and let them do the marketing. Do like you do with the Dairy Commission. They are appointed by the government. I asked why they should want that, and they say; "Because that is the best security any farm producer has. We don't mind seeing that for chickens, we don't mind seeing that for eggs, and we wouldn't mind seeing that for pork."
But I am a strong believer in producers running their own organizations, and that is the reason why I have been very reluctant to move in that direction. I believe in democracy though the member for Crowfoot says I do not. He would not dare go out into Saskatchewan and tell them to get rid of the Wheat Board. But those people who run the Wheat Board are appointed by the government. For the first time in history they elected a group of advisers to the Board, if you want to call them that. I am not suggesting we should go that far, but it has been suggested to me that this is the kind of efficient marketing system that we need in Canada.
I only used pork as an example of what history shows. It always shows it is not a great economic benefit to society, either producers or consumers, this up and down effect. It doesn't necessarily have to be in there because this up and down effect means an up and down income for the farmers of the nation. Their investments today are too high for them to continue to tolerate that type of thing.
When the hon. member talks about world markets, about Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba competing for markets such as Japan, the only contracts which were honoured or, I should say, the only guaranteed pork sales they had at a constant price, were the contracts with Japan which were honoured. They completely jumped off the market when the energy crisis took place in the world and they had to spend more of their money on energy. The government affected concluded that its people could get along without certain products so they removed themselves from the free pork market. But they did honour the contracts they had. It meant, though, that buying power disappeared by 50 per cent.
A ministerial delegation is going to Japan in the latter part of next week to talk about these various things-to make sure that we can continue our supplies. Perhaps someone can come up with a better system, a better system which will guarantee some of the things our producers want.
I have talked to many people in Canada. I have gone outside this chamber to talk to many people, not only farmers but urban people also, to find out what their views are, what they think about agriculture.

I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, about three weeks ago at a dinner meeting in Toronto I was sitting next to the Mayor of Toronto. He said: "I don't know what you are talking about, but I can tell you if I were running as a leader for a certain party in this country I would certainly run on stabilization, because everybody in the cities thinks it is a wonderful idea that you are going to guarantee people food at stable prices with a decent return to farmers. I am an urbanite and I know nothing about farming, but if I was the leader of a party I would steal that policy from you; you have convinced the people of Canada that it is necessary, and after seeing you on television I believe it is the answer myself."
I said: "Mr. Mayor, if you listen to the farm organizations and talk to the rural people you will realize how important this is, even more so if you go to world food meetings and hear what they are demanding by way of a constant supply of food; you just don't produce food and hope that somebody is going to buy it, or produce huge surpluses which will be held over your head like a club so that you can be beaten down in price."
I am surprised the hon. member for Crowfoot and the other member from the same province would talk about these things. They come from part of Canada where the producers of grain held 30 per cent of the world's grain reserves. They were held over their heads like a club. They could not even afford to buy decent clothes for their children or to pay their taxes because they held those tremendous grain reserves for the free markets of the world, and could not get rid of them.

Mr. Speaker, I could have interrupted the hon. member for Crowfoot when he was talking about the letter that he wrote to the young farmer some place in Manitoba. I am sure that he would give an honest interpretation of what was said by the Minister of Agriculture for Canada, but I am also sure I could have helped him a little in writing that letter.
I am not going to take up much more time of the House, but I do want to say something about world conditions as they apply to Canadian producers. The commodities that we sell will be in greater demand on world markets. However, what are world markets doing with other products, such as energy, cocoa beans or coffee beans? Countries are forming cartels so they can bargain with the rest of the world to ensure they are not taken advantage of. We have to recognize that we will have to be part of that world or suffer the consequences. We will not be able to deal much differently with them.
Agricultural Stabilization Act
Let us go to the European community and see how they operate with their so-called free trade system. For example, if you ship a cargo to Europe, when it enters the harbour they can slap a levy on it if they do not want it. I suggest that we have one of the freest trade systems in the world. This is why I am alarmed at this talk of curtailing agriculture, and at people who put this idea across the country when I know that they are fully knowledgeable of what we are doing in Canada in terms of trade in agricultural products and the possibilities that exist. I also know fully well that in light of world conditions we have to take immediate action.
The acceptability of motion No. 4, as far as I am concerned, is out of the question. This amendment in the bill was designed to provide an opportunity for the government, following discussions with the provinces, to provide for methods of stabilization for producers which would involve actions other than purchase, deficiency payments, and payments for the benefit of producers now provided under section 10 of the act. It is true that the amendment is general and that it can be considered to give the Governor in Council broad power. But with the need for food production and stability in the agricultural sector, it is important to have adequate power to meet unforeseen situations in this important sector. The basic reason for the amendment is to enable us to act and react immediately.
I do not know whether anyone would suggest that I or any other Minister of Agriculture would abuse these powers, but we have an amendment in the bill providing for consultation with the producers of the nation before action is taken. I have been a strong believer in consultation with the producers of the nation.
I was also requested in committee to restate some of my feelings to the House when the bill came up at report stage and third reading. Concern was expressed about the possibility that, despite the safeguards in subsection 10( 1) (a) and (b), a province might decide to topload the federal stabilization program on a given commodity, making it more profitable to produce that commodity in that province as compared to other provinces that also produce the commodity. I assure the House that in such a situation, under the amendment the Governor in Council would be of the opinion that such toploading would be to the disadvantage of the other provinces, and would have to say that no toploading would be permitted unless all four provinces producing the commodity were in agreement in regard to that kind of toploading program. I suggest it would simply create more inequity and inequality, and as Minister of Agriculture for Canada I do not want to see that happen.
For example, under the Canadian Dairy Commission we have practically eliminated the inequality that used to exist between producers producing the same commodity for the same market. There is now very little variance in the price of industrial milk across the nation. Only two or three years ago it varied by as much as $3 per hundredweight because there was an invisible provincial line. That has now been almost eliminated as a result of Canadian farmers, provincial ministers of agriculture, and Canadian farm organizations working together. Let me reassure the House through you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not my inten-

Agricultural Stabilization Act
tion to become a dictator to Canadian agriculture, because I know that would not work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate under the guise of speaking to an amendment at the report stage. The minister has just stated how he would like to be a socialist, though he does not want to become one by the exercise of undue control. The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) indicated that, while he does not want to be a dictator, either, he would like to see some form of dictatorship that would result in stable prices. The argument then turned to whether or not we have supply management.
The interesting philosophical part of this bill came from the remarks made by the hon. member for Crowfoot regarding why we have Bill C-50 as well as Bill C-41. If we were to amend this bill on third reading to include the six commodities covered under the other stabilization bill, the situation would be very interesting. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) would then be responsible for stabilizing all farm products, and we would eliminate what has become a great problem for the Liberal party, with its members travelling around the country, and we could turn our attention to arriving at some kind of arrangement for those six commodities referred to in Bill C-41.
Bill C-41 obviously has nothing to do with supply management, because supply management has been used ever since the Wheat Board was set up. The commodities designated by the bill have always been on a quota system and require a different kind of supply management than that talked about by the minister and the hon. member for Crowfoot.
The Minister of Agriculture fails to realize something that he used to know, and that is that the way to stabilize farm prices is to pay the farmers a fair price for their products. If price parity is achieved on agricultural commodities, then there will be reasonable amount of interest on the part of the farmers to produce those commodities. In fact, if you pay them sufficient to enable the farmers to do reasonably well, quite often they will provide the Canadian public with a surplus of those commodities.
Therein lies the problem. Some people think of supply management in terms of one person farming only 300 acres of a certain commodity, or raising 200 head of cattle, or paying a premium on 1,500 hogs, and toploading in one province with payment of a large additional amount. If we were to forget that kind of antiquated argument over supply management and go back to what is fundamental to every farmer and every commodity in every part of Canada, that is, a decent price for the product, then we would be able to stabilize prices and encourage the farmers to stay on the land. Perhaps we would then be able to do what the minister brags we are doing, but which we are not going to do unless the prices are stabilized. We are not going to be able to meet the commitments the Minister of Agriculture made in Rome at the World Food Conference unless the individual farmer gets enough money that he can stay on the land.

It was interesting to hear the Minister of Agriculture say he disagrees violently with his counterpart, the minister of agriculture for Ontario. It is true that Ontario has gone into all kinds of marketing legislation and that some of that legislation is highly directed to management. It is a fact that if you are a grower of tobacco in Ontario you are told you must only put in a certain number of acres, you must only harvest a certain amount of the product, and you will receive a certain price. Ontario has done very well in this regard, and there has been very little complaint from the farmer.
There are other sections of agriculture under very strict quota systems in Ontario, and some of these restrictions have worked very well. There are many marketing boards in the country, I believe in the neighbourhood of 80 altogether, many of which have no quota structure or limitations at all. These are just boards set up for mutual protection, mutual advertising of the product, and to make arrangements about how to go after sales. These boards do not worry very much about prices of commodities in the marketplace.
The Minister of Agriculture has said he disagrees with the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, and that he believes his representation, made under rather special circumstances to the committee, was made for the purpose of intervening in respect of the top-loading provision written into this bill. To be fair to the minister of agriculture for Ontario, he was right in this regard, because he really was the only one representing a province that could use top-loading in respect of almost everything.
It is fair to suggest, I believe, that the province of British Columbia is top-loading now in respect of cattle. It had to do so for a very simple reason. British Columbia has a relatively small amount of arable land. That province decided this land should not become subject to speculation but should remain in agricultural production. To keep the people in agricultural production the province had to agree to provide the farmers with a decent standard of living. The province held out the carrot in British Columbia, and even the free enterprisers in the cattle industry were willing to accept it because the carrot was sizeable.
This action on the part of British Columbia will, in all likelihood, have an eventual adverse effect on the rest of the cattle industry, and I presume that is why so many officials of that industry are interested in talking to members of parliament at this time.
If I thought the hon. member for Crowfoot was right in his assertion that this part of the bill will give the Minister of Agriculture power to decide the price, the quantity, and virtually all aspects of supply management policy in respect of the six commodities referred to in Bill C-41, I would be inclined to support the minister.
The hon. member for Crowfoot has said very often that the real criterion to be used in measuring how well a farmer is getting along is the price he is paid for his commodity at the farm gate, and that if he does not get enough at the farm gate to pay his input costs of running the operation he will not be in business.
June 11, 1975

Whether we accomplish this aim by holding out a carrot, as we did ih respect of the dairy commission, or in some other way, it must be accomplished. The only thing the federal government can be proud of in its whole damned stabilization policy for the last 17 years is the creation of the Canadian Dairy Commission, particularly the industrial milk section. This has been the only solution the government has found to any of the farmers' problems, or this is the only solution that has proven successful. This is the only commission which has been able to carry on as a separate entity.
The government has helped out hog producers and egg producers, it has helped out the hens, the sheep and the wool producers. The government has helped all the animals and all the farmers, but it has not solved very many of their problems. If the hon. member for Crowfoot really believes that by giving the minister this kind of power we will be giving him complete autocratic control, let me say that I for one would much rather it be given to this minister than the minister who will have autocratic control as a result of Bill C-41. I would like this Minister of Agriculture to be given the power to set floor prices and establish a marketing structure that would guarantee a reasonable price for those products covered by Bill C-41.
One of the major problems that has faced Canadians in past years has been the result of surplus agricultural production. Surely this must be of concern to many members of this House. Every time you turn on your television these days you see a picture of children starving in some part of this world, yet every time we have had difficulties in the agricultural industry they have been the result of over-production following prices reaching parity with production costs.
With very few exceptions, in a few selective areas, it has been impossible for farmers to become wealthy. It has often been said that western farmers all have airplanes and fly south every winter. I think this is a myth that has been spread in eastern Canada over a long period of time. Whenever I have been in western Canada I have found that the farmers do not live in better houses, certainly do not have better buildings, and I do not believe they have better incomes than farmers in other parts of Canada. This indicates perhaps that farmers all across Canada do not receive enough for their products. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Certainly we do not have a sufficient number of farmers in Canada today to utilize fully our agricultural potential.
The minister speaks of his desire to be able to meet these needs. I am personally aware that he has made some very socialistic statements in the past. He has made some statements which have put him in bad stead with some of his colleagues. He indicated he looked very favourably at the cooperatives, and at the matter of western farmers getting together to decide the amount they should produce of their own commodity in order to maintain the price. Therefore, if the board should see fit to give the minister the right to increase his control over any of these commodities and the end result should be a parity price for the farmers, I would think another department would have to have responsibility for the distribution. There are even in
Agricultural Stabilization Act
this country many needy persons who still require the abundance of agricultural products we can produce.
The Agricultural Stabilization Act over the last 15 or 16 years by various means has bailed out farmers who have been in desperate need with relation to many commodities. It established stability, but stability is almost like welfare. The stabilizaton was at a very low level so that the farmer would not lose his farm, but it was not high enough that the farmer could do very much on the farm.
I am pleased to see that the new legislation contains changes which, in my opinion, are advantageous and which will guarantee that the price the farmer will receive will be 90 per cent of the average over the last five years. This will be indexed to his costs.
I suggest to the people in western Canada who are now being asked to consider Bill C-41 that, if this bill is successful, any commodity may be designated under this bill, even those included in some sections of the other bill. If we are successful I believe we will not only stabilize the welfare level in respect of agricultural commodities but that the minister will have the potential to develop at least 70 per cent or 80 per cent of the capacity in that field. He will have an obligation to sell the commodities. I believe that all this bill should do is supply the farmer with a floor price at a level that would keep him in business.
Very shortly we should look at a farm incomes program separate from welfare. We should decide what type of a program we should have in order to keep the farmer in business and make his contribution to the agricultural production of Canada. We should decide what the program should be in the North American economy and what it should be in respect of the international world food bank. When we make those decisions we will also have to make a decision that farm land should be retained as agricultural producing land.
We should have a farm income program which would ensure that the farmer would be able to have his weekends free and provide for his old age, while at the same time enjoying the amenities of life similar to those enjoyed by other segments of our economy. If the minister can do this within the authority he is being given by this legislation- and I believe he could if he so wished-then I am quite prepared to support the clause which has been written in, and I do not share the fears of the hon. member for Crowfoot who, I believe, is of the opinion that the minister really cannot produce the type of supply management that would in effect end up as an income guarantee for the farmers in any given situation.

Madam Speaker, it is without any reservation that I support the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). I was rather alarmed when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) took a few partisan political chops at the hon. member for Crowfoot.
Up until 1972 I was involved in the business sector of agriculture. I was not involved in politics. Having been involved in business, I really know what this is all about since I was engaged in the business of marketing livestock. The only people who would listen to us in those days were the right hon. member for Prince Albert, (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. member for Crowfoot, and a few others on this side of the House. I believe people involved

June 11, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
in agriculture, especially in western Canada and in the maritimes. are particularly grateful to the hon. member for Crowfoot and many others who fought the very dictatorial legislation contained in Bill C-176.
So that the Minister of Agriculture will have an idea how the people in the west and in the maritimes feel, I should like to refer to the Globe and Mail for March 8 and on an article written by James Rusk. This article states that the beef producers in Canada, and in the United States for that matter, have traditionally fought government involvement in the industry with the same ferocity with which they battled coyotes, blizzards, and rustlers. It goes on to state that the people are angered that one of their number, a former federal agricultural minister, H. A. Olson, had the temerity to mention beef cattle in the legislation to create national marketing agencies. It is suggested that this was a major factor in his defeat in the 1972 federal election in the southern Alberta cow country constituency of Medicine Hat. I think that is pretty indicative of the way free enterprisers in agriculture think today.
I do not believe it would be right for me to condemn the Minister of Agriculture, unjustly, but I think it is right if I am to do a job for the people in my constituency that I should look over the record of the Minister of Agriculture since he came to office.
In February, 1973, as a budget measure to combat inflation Canada removed its import tariff of three cents a pound on beef and one and a half cents a pound on live cattle. That was a move taken by the Minister of Agriculture. On March 29, 1973, the United States government imposed price controls on food products. On August 2,
1973,	Canada imposed controls on exports. On September 9, 1973, the United States ended the freeze on beef prices. On September 14, 1973, Canada lifted its export controls. On September 21, 1973, Canada re-instated the tariff. On November 2, 1973, Canada adopted a temporary surcharge which was removed on February 10, 1974. On March 15,
1974,	Canada announced a subsidy program. On April 9, 1974, Canada banned all imports containing DES. On August 12, 1974, the U.S. and Canada agreed upon DES certification program and Canada announced a global import quota system. On November 16, 1974, the U.S. declared quotas on Canadian livestock and products. The source for this information is the Food Prices Review Board, and various publications where this can be found.
The minister is asking for more power. He has all the power he needs. I spoke about the actions taken by him and, as stated in the bill, by the Governor in Council. Unfortunately when we see who the Governor in Council is we find it happens to be the Cabinet. As we look at the seating order, we find that there is not one person in the Cabinet who is involved with agriculture. So I do not think we can really condemn the Minister of Agriculture because his hands are tied and he has no alternative.

Would the hon. member permit a question? I thought I heard the hon. member say that there was no person with experience in agriculture on this side. I know of at least two of my colleagues, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) and the Minister of Agriculture,

who have had that experience, quite apart from the experience which some others of us have.
My question really is with regard to all the action which the government took with regard to beef, which the hon. member listed. I wonder if the hon. member will recognize that during the course of that period those various government actions widened considerably the spread in the price for beef between the Omaha market and the Canadian market, and therefore acted very much to the advantage of the Canadian producer. Does he not agree that it would be fair to comment on the wisdom of those actions rather than just enumerate them, when they resulted in this wide spread in favour of Canadian producers?

speechtext:
The minister spoke in reply to a question of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). I am sure he is aware the hon. minister is a farmer who owns 200 acres of land, but he has been involved in local politics for 35 years while his brother ran the farm. In order to become familiar with agriculture, you have to be involved in it at all times.
In his opening remarks the minister said the hon. member for Crowfoot has accused him of not knowing anything about free enterprise. It seems to me that he has divorced himself from that because we all know it is the Minister of Agriculture who advocates marketing boards and who believes in supply management. We all know what comes next. There will be quotas, and after quotas government takeover and government control. This is what we are afraid of.
The minister referred to Alberta and state control in Alberta. They never go on to tell you that Alberta's gas trunk line shares are held by people in central Canada. He also referred to Saskatchewan. I think the proof will be in the election tonight. We have had a mass exodus of people from Saskatchewan, as I found out during the last election. Exploration work in Saskatchewan is at a standstill, and the people of Saskatchewan will show what they think in the election tonight.
I did not want to speak on the amendment of the hon. member for Crowfoot, or get into an argument with any of the ministers. I am just stating facts. It is our duty to look at the record before we condemn anyone. Here are the last figures since the Minister of Agriculture took office and during his tenure. According to those figures, our exports of meat have dropped by 19.4 per cent, our exports of dairy products have dropped by 49.3 per cent, our exports of fruit have dropped by 20.7 per cent, and our exports of vegetables have dropped by 9.5 per cent. Those were the figures given to me by the external trade division in answer to a question on the Order Paper this week.
Another thing that concerns me is the extra power asked for by the minister. He is asking for more and more power, although he already has all the power necessary under the present act. Why he wants that power, I do not know, and the reason I hesitate to give him any more power is the
June 11, 1975

record which I have just read. I do not think there is any minister who has done worse during his tenure of office than the present minister.
Recently I paid a visit to a communist country with a group of parliamentarians. There was the odd person in the group who thought this was a pretty good way of life. I give government members credit because they were not among them. We had a very enjoyable time, but we saw the way communism worked, we saw the government take over 70 per cent of the land, we saw government control, we saw the government force private people off the farms, and we saw production drop.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

speechtext: This sounds like Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: The Minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) is in a pretty jovial mood, but I would like to point out to him what will happen if we allow this to happen. I should like to quote from a letter written by a person from the minister's province. I do not know whether he has ever heard of Rabbit Lake, Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
It appeared in the Western Producer of Thursday, May 22, 1975, and it was written by Mrs. Alice Krilow of Rabbit Lake, Saskatchewan. Here is what she thinks will happen if we continue with government controls and takeovers. The letter is entitled, "Land Bank Critic". She wrote:
I notice Mr. John J. Mitchell never gives up. We hashed the Land Bank over in the News Optimist, North Battleford and lo and behold I pick up The Western Producer and there is Mr. Mitchell again.
First, Mr. Mitchell, why don't you inform everyone you are a retired school teacher not a farmer.
Second, you have no right to tell farmers what is good for them. Retiring farmers in luxury on taxpayers dollars and sinking young people into government ownership is never going to keep our province going on or the world fed. Have you ever stopped to think about what the future will be with everyone working for the government? That is communism.
Why doesn't the government go into the house building and buying business then everyone can rent their houses and never worry about mortgages or owning their own homes? If this kind of life is good for farmers let's make it good for "everyone".
I am a farmer's wife, I know all about hard work and doing without many things other people take for granted, but I still like the security of knowing if anything happens to my husband, I and my children will have something left to keep our bellies full. What would we have if this land were rented from the government, a welfare cheque?
I tell you that these are the feelings of people all across the country. During my visit to the Maritimes last week I found that people in farm communities in the Maritimes feel the same as we do in western Canada. I do not know how to describe the way they feel down there regarding agriculture-they feel that central Canada, Ottawa especially, has agriculture pulling on the cow's horns. They think western Canada is pulling on the cow's tail. The Minister of Agriculture, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) are milking her dry. That is what is happening today, Madam Speaker.
I feel sorry for some members who came to this House in 1972 when I did, and for those who came in 1974. I always
Agricultural Stabilization Act
felt the greatest people I ever met were the people in agriculture in my own little corner of the world. Since I have been in Ottawa, however, I know that some of the finest people I have ever met are in this House of Commons and they come from all parts of the country. I have met some wonderful people here who would really like to do the job they said they would do during the elections when they were out on the hustings. I do not know whether it is the Prime Minister, the party whip, the Minister of Agriculture, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board or who is responsible, but when it comes time to vote they are whipped into shape and vote against what their constituents want.
I believe the government is void of ideas and that is why we have rules and regulations and controls. We do not even feed Canadian beef to our armed service personnel in Europe. We have 707s flying over there all the time, but we buy beef from the United States and Denmark to feed them. We have been in a surplus position, but our exports have dropped by 19.3 per cent during the term of the present Minister of Agriculture.
The government claims that it has consulted and listened to every segment of the industry, but that is not so. The Canadian Cattlemen's Association urged that adequate changes be made in the federal taxation of producers and said this would be superior to any ad hoc subsidy scheme. They proposed the capital herd concept which is in practice in the United States. This puts an investment value on cattle and provides the same kind of tax treatment for livestock as for most other capital investment. They recommended certain tax provisions to ensure the transfer of the family farm to children as a viable economic unit. Madam Speaker, these are ways to stabilize and to encourage young people to stay on the farm.
The Minister of Agriculture talked about implementing the beef subsidy program. We have a guaranteed price of 45.32 cents per pound but nobody in agriculture is going to collect a penny. We have begged the minister to go to Washington to lobby with Secretary Butz because the trade patterns in this country are north and south. Every time there is a confrontation with the United States market Canada is going to be the loser. I am not antiAmerican but I am pro-Canadian. I think it is our duty to get along with our neighbours whether they are across a barbed wire fence or across the longest undefended border in the world.
It is our duty to do everything to encourage the minister to lobby with our greatest trading partner in order to build markets. I think that stabilization is selling. The minister goes to Toronto and tells them that their foodstuff is cheaper than in any other country in the world, and then the next day he tells producers they are going to receive more for their products. I want to conclude by saying that I am happy to support the motion of the hon. member for Crowfoot.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to remind the House that the agricultural prices stabilization bill is a stop loss type of legislation. It is there to give the farmer a guarantee that if there is a drop in prices he will have a floor. Under the rules in the marketplace this bill simply modifies the
6670

June 11, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
price; that is all it does. In spite of all the debate this afternoon this is not a supply management bill. All it does is give a floor price, which is an indication to the farmer that he is to produce more or less according to that floor price. In that respect it has an impact on supply.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) was correct when he said it is not a supply management bill nor is the Wheat Board a supply management operation. It simply sets the price. All farmers accept this. Where the clash of opinion comes is on the question of what, since the war, has been called supply management. The idea arose in Europe after the war. It came to the United States in the 1960's, and to Canada in the 1970's.
I would point out to the House again that this bill is not a supply management bill. It is a fundamental part of the package that you must have as an agricultural policy to make the system work. It is a device to stabilize prices by setting in advance a floor which indicates to the farmer what he should do about production by price and not by control.
Where the trouble arises, and what prompted the amendment of the hon. member for Crowfoot, is that the minister in this House and in committee keeps bringing up the question of supply management. The great majority of farmers honestly believe that they want governments to get off their backs. They would like to make their own decisions. All they want from government is some aid to stabilize income without changing the fundamental laws of supply and demand.
I understand the amendment of the hon. member for Crowfoot because I was in committee when the words "supply management" came up in discussion. They were brought in gratuitously by the minister. They have no bearing on the bill, however.
I know this bill, Madam Speaker. I helped draft the original in 1958. This bill is not the answer to all the problems of farmers; it is only one step in a process, one part of a package. All we are doing at this stage is dealing with the Conservative legislation of 16 or 17 years ago and hopefully making it better. The fundamentals are the same.
It is true that under this bill the minister has discretionary powers, and we have to trust him not to abuse those powers. It is this talk of supply management in connection with the bill which has alarmed hon. members from farming areas.
Somebody mentioned the election is Saskatchewan today. It is a provincial election, but the issue that is bothering people is having government get off their backs. According to information I have, when the polls opened this morning, people were lined up waiting to go in. Somebody is going to catch it tonight. When I hear of people lining up to enter the polls in the morning, I know-knowing Saskatchewan as I do-that somebody is going to get it.
The possibility of the government being on the backs of the people is frightening the people. There is no need to raise such issues; as the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Hurlburt) said, these things can be done the proper way. If

you want to sell your goods, you have to help the other chap sell his; only in that way can he earn the money with which to buy your goods.
I come now to the bill and the amendment. When the bill was being considered in committee two main concerns were raised by members of all parties. One had to do with the so-called top loading provision, the provision which would give the minister power to make deals with other provinces and producers, and establish a floor above the formula price. The inherent danger in the top loading provision was well illustrated by the minister from Ontario who made a valuable presentation. I think it is fair to say that all members of all parties supported the position of the minister from Ontario and, at their suggestion, I suggested amendments which have been included in this bill, as reprinted, on page 4.
In that committee I assured the minister that I would, on behalf of my party, support amendments brought in by the government in response to our request. Those amendments were intended to remove certain fears that two or three rich provinces could top load any particular industry or product and thereby harm other provinces and producers.
The amendments on page 4 were brought in by the government at our request. The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) still expressed some concern, and the minister promised that, when he speaks in the House, he will make an unequivocal statement to the effect that if two or three of our provinces should support top loading policies, the federal government will have no part or share of such top loading.
Top loading, to those who are not familiar with the term, is the means by which wealthy provinces like B.C., Alberta, Ontario, and possibly Saskatchewan establish supports which are much higher than those other provinces can afford. The effect is this: top loading diminishes and even destroys producers in other provinces which cannot provide that type of support. In the interests of maintaining a healthy agriculture in all parts of Canada, the members of all parties making up the committee agreed that top loading should not be used as an incentive.
Let me read the amendment into the record. I am about to read from page 4 of the revised version of the bill, and I shall begin quoting at line 30. The amendment says that the minister may enter into an agreement ... unless he is of the opinion that such an agreement
(a)	would give to the producers of the commodity who are to be parties to the agreement or for whose benefit the agreement would be entered into, a financial advantage in the production or marketing of the commodity not enjoyed by other producers of the commodity in Canada;-
In plain terms, the law says that the minister cannot make an agreement if it gives some producers an advantage over others. I thank the minister for accepting that amendment which was suggested by the opposition. The amended clause goes on to say:
-or
(b)	would be an incentive to the producers of the commodity who are to be parties to the agreement or for whose benefit the agreement would be entered into, to over-produce the commodity.
The two parts I just read were added to the bill at the request of the opposition, and were supported by every
June 11, 1975

member of the committee. I declare my support for them now, on behalf of the party I represent.
The second concern has to do with the particular amendment we are considering today. Some hon. members found subclause 5(2) of the original version frightening. After we had discussed it in committee and heard the full story, we did not find it nearly so frightening. Listen to the language of subclause 5(2)(1.1) as proposed in the original version:
For the purpose of stabilizing the price of an agricultural commodity, the board may exercise such other powers as are prescribed by the Governor in Council for that purpose.
It sounds as if there is no limitation to the power of the board, and that alarmed not only the members of the committee but various farm organizations and several provinces. Once again the opposition suggested an amendment. We suggested that the powers under that clause should be used only after consultation with producers. Then departmental officials said that you cannot have producers advising the Cabinet. Consequently we suggested the insertion of an amendment in clause 2 on page 2. The reprinted version of clause 2 of the bill reads in part:
-after consultation with producer groups, recommendations respecting the powers that may be prescribed under subsection 10(1.1), as are necessary-
I accepted, on behalf of the group I represented in committee, that amendment which was suggested by officials, and I re-affirm my party's support of that amendment.
Having said that, I must report to the House that the hon. member for Crowfoot was not satisfied; he wanted to see the reprinted version of the bill; he was not satisfied that the suggested amendments would meet his objection. He feared, that the minister Still possessed increased or unlimited powers. Consequently he brought forward his amendment.
For my part, I do not share the hon. member's concern about this particular bill. I can see the logic of what he says; however, having read the bill, and knowing the bill as I do, I have come to the conclusion that the clause he is worried about does not relate to supply management powers. To understand this matter, one should refer to the old act which made available to the board three techniques for stabilizing price.
Obviously the provinces and producers discussed the possibility of the government's producing techniques other than those originally brought forward in 1958-59. Knowing that this clause refers to techniques, rather than to the theory of supply management, a theory which opposes pricing under a free market system and which espouses control of production, and being aware of the historical background of the clause, I am not so worried about it. It simply gives power to the Governor in Council, on recommendation of the board, to propose new techniques. Previously this had to be done in consultation with the farmers. Therefore, having read the bill, I am willing to accept the assurance that this is not a supply management clause.
I am willing to accept the minister's word that he will not be dictatorial and I therefore assure the minister, or the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), who is here in his place, that I will honour the commitment I made in com-
Agricultural Stabilization Act
mittee. My party and I find the government's version acceptable.
I must raise a little problem now-if I could get the minister's attention for a moment. The minister had given his word to look into a problem which is bothering the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte. The minister said he would make a statement on the hypothetical example quoted by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte. He said if that circumstance occurred when he was minister, he would not allow it. That concerned the two or three provinces overloading, and the federal government participating. I would like the Minister of Justice to convey to the Minister of Agriculture that he should give that assurance to the hon. member as he promised, because that is the closest we will get to having it in legislation.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the short time left in this debate on the report stage of Bill C-50, I want to make some comments related mainly to the top loading feature. Before doing that I want to say how disappointed I was when the commodity wool was no longer allowed to be included as part of the named commodities in this bill.
The sheep and wool industry is the forgotten agricultural commodity in Canada today. It has been for some time, perhaps as far back as World War II. It was a sad day for Canada's sheep and wool industry when the government, under the previous Minister of Agriculture, wiped out the wool deficiency program. That was the last straw for an already struggling commodity group in Canada.
The reason suggested by the present minister and the former deputy minister of agriculture was very unrealistic and inappropriate, to say the least. The reason was that the wool deficiency program had to be dropped because it was not accomplishing the original objective, presumably to encourage the sheep and wool industry in Canada. How could it? It was not given a chance.
That action was the final blow, and still further depressed our sheep and wool industry. It was most noticed by those producers of sheep and wool along the United States border, especially in western Canada, because that policy was in sharp contrast to the subsidized sheep and wool industry across the border in the northwest United States such as Montana and Wyoming. The omission of wool is a very serious aspect. It is too bad it is not included in the bill.
I want to come now to the matter of top loading. It is the most important aspect of Bill C-50. I want to refer in
particular to a very significant meeting, one which the minister referred to in his remarks. I refer to the meeting of the British Columbia Cattlemen's Association held in Kamloops on May 22. It was the two-way annual convention of that association. The biggest issue by far was the matter of income assurance as applied to the beef commodity group.
I attended for two and a half days in order to observe. It has been many years since I have seen a debate in the field of agriculture similar to that. It lasted four hours or more and became very emotional. There was a very tense atmosphere. In spite of that, there was a very high level of debate on the part of those who debated the pros and cons.
The only other similar situation I can remember was in 1952 or 1953 when we first debated the issue of compulsory marketing boards in Canada. In particular I think of a meeting in the Palliser Hotel in Calgary. The same atmosphere prevailed and there was a very tense and emotional debate.
I want to preface my remarks about this British Columbia income assurance program for cattle by saying that my interest at that meeting and my remarks today relate strictly to the impact of a top loading plan such as this and the impact it might have on a national agricultural commodity that is involved in international trade, especially with the United States. May I call it six o'clock, Madam Speaker.
